paper_title: Increasing isotropy and predictability through electroplating of tensile properties of polyamide 12 parts manufactured by selective laser sintering
text_for_embedding:
[s40964-025-01386-w | Additive Manufacturing / Materials | Abstract | N/A]
Abstract
Additive manufacturing is rapidly evolving and finding a place in nearly every industry. Recent advances make selective laser 
sintering especially well positioned to rapidly create complex parts with material properties capable of withstanding rigorous 
end use applications. However, these properties still pale in comparison to their metal powder bed fusion counterparts and 
can be plagued by anisotropy due to print orientation. This can be especially true for large parts with relatively thin structural 
walls. Combining selective laser sintering with metal electroplating has shown promise to increase both strength and isotropy. 
While traditional metal–polymer hybrid composites have struggled to maintain consistent properties across varying geometries, 
this work demonstrates control over material properties at scales previously not possible, enabling a new class of lightweight 
structures with improved survivability. This novel research has experimentally found the tensile properties and isotropy of different electroplating coatings and investigates techniques that can be used to increase coating adhesion and uniformity over the 
rough non-conductive printed part surface. It is shown that though both the printed and electroplated material are individually 
anisotropic, the combination of printing and subsequent electroplating can improve overall build direction isotropy. This research 
represents a shift in additive manufacturing by transforming what was once considered a limitation of SLS printing—thin-wall 
anisotropy—into an opportunity for creating customized material properties through strategic metal deposition but also opens 
up new design spaces where minimum weight and minimum volume design trajectories are needed.

section: 1 Introduction Polymers have found application in nearly every industry (Part 1/4)

[s40964-025-01386-w | Additive Manufacturing / Materials | 1 Introduction Polymers have found application in nearly every industry (Part 1/4) | p.3]
1 Introduction
Polymers have found application in nearly every industry 
[1] and additive manufacturing (AM) has been a critical 
manufacturing method used to expand polymer applications. Powder bed fusion (PBF) is an AM method with proven 
success in creating complex parts and within PBF selective 
laser sintering (SLS) is an established method capable of 
creating end use polymer parts [2, 3]. Within this manufacturing method, polymamide-12 (PA12) is one of the most 
cost-effective materials due to its reliability, durability, and 
chemical resistance [4, 5]. PA12 is specifically well suited 
for laser sintering because of the relatively low sintering 
power requirements, high material refresh ratios, and ability 
to print without an inert chamber [6, 7]. SLS can also produce highly intricate, nested, and lightweight parts without 
the use of support material at extremely competitive cost 
compared to traditional manufacturing methods. Even though SLS with PA12 can produce end use parts at 
a fraction of the price and weight of metal PBF, the strength 
of PA12 parts cannot compete with metal PBF. Metal parts 
often have higher wear resistance, thermal resilience, and 
electrical conductivity. Polymer parts are also susceptible 
to UV, hygroscopicity, and degradation when exposed to 
other liquid media [8, 9]. Another common detrimental biproduct of PA12 PBF is anisotropy of the part based on build 
orientation and part thickness [10–14]. Electroplating is a 
well-established procedure that is poised to not only mitigate 
many of the undesirable environmental effects on polymers 
but also increase the strength of polymers [15–19]. Electroplating continues to play a more critical role in AM with 
research and implementation skyrocketing in recent years 
[20, 21]. Much of the progress in combining AM and electroplating (often referred to as hybrid AM or HAM) involves 
selectively depositing conductive material to make 2D and 
3D circuit boards [22–25]. Electroplating also combines the 
benefits of low weight polymers with the benefits of metal 
surfaces due to the minimal thickness of the metal coating [15, 16, 26, 27]. With such broad advantages of electroplating, this technology has found use in nearly every 
industry to include automotive, electronics, aviation, oil and 
gas, air conditioning, toy and jewelry manufacturing, and 
national defense [21]. None of the found research employs 
electroplating with AM to address issues of AM print anisotropy. Simonson et al. did investigate using electroplating 
to decrease layer-to-layer debonding of fused filament parts 
but found electroplating polylactic acid parts manufactured 
through fused deposition modeling actually weakened the 
tensile properties by approximately 20% [28]. Zarybnicka 
et al. demonstrated similar results with sintered PA12 if 
additives are added to the powder prior to sintering which 
can result in a decrease of tensile properties of the final part 
and little effect on part anisotropy due to print orientation 
[29]. This research investigates novel techniques to incorporate electroplating into the PA12 PBF process to address 
polymer environmental degradation, strength, and anisotropy issues while maintaining total manufacture cost and 
end part weight at a fraction of the metal counterpart. This is 
particularly true with thin-walled (< 1 mm) SLS structures.

The present research also demonstrates the ability to use the 
rule of mixtures (ROM) to predict and customize material 
properties based on coating type and volume fraction. Electroplating non-metallic parts holds its own challenges; however, when the parts also have rough nonuniform surfaces found on SLS parts, the challenges are 
compounded and often result in poor bonding at the polymer–metal interface [17, 29–31]. Baligidad et al. found poor 
bonding at the metal interface was detrimental to mechanical 
properties of the end part [8]. Methods to address the first 
challenge of creating a conductive material to include surface embedding conductive material in the polymer, precoating the part with an adhesive spray, and treating the surface 
with an electroless coating have all been met with mixed 
success [8, 16, 17, 19, 22, 24]. Creating a relatively smooth 
surface is the second common challenge and attempts to 
mitigate this are often done through mechanical methods 
chemical changes or a combination of these two methods

[s40964-025-01386-w | Additive Manufacturing / Materials | 1 Introduction Polymers have found application in nearly every industry (Part 3/4) | p.3]
[17, 30–32]. Some studies have also found that the adhesion 
of a metal coating on laser sintered PA12 and the continuity 
and uniformity of follow on metal coatings was increased by 
starting with a thin layer of Cu [8, 17]
This research has employed a unique order of electroplating to achieve uniform adhesion and thickness at the 
material interface. The research community and some commercial entities [16, 30] have done extensive testing of electroplating AM parts and have found that SLS prints generally have a great deal of surface variability. This can be seen 
to a lesser degree with other AM printing methods, such as 
stereolithography (SLA) and multijet fusion (MJF). A very 
simple screening test is to weigh parts prior to plating to 
look for porosity. The weight in grams of a part divided by 
the part’s volume, which can be read from the 3D model, 
gives an indication up front if the part is porous. A dimensional check on the printed part must also be done to ensure 
the printed part size matches the 3D model. The part weight 
in grams (g) divided by its volume in cubic centimeters (cc) 
should be very close to 1 for PA12 parts. PA12 parts whose 
density is below 0.95 g/cc often will have issues of staining 
and will likely be weaker as well. It is also essential that 
there are no residual powders on the parts. While traditional metal–polymer hybrid composites have 
struggled to maintain consistent properties across varying 
geometries, this work in electroplating SLS parts demonstrates control over material properties at scales previously 
not possible, enabling a new class of lightweight structures 
with improved survivability. The ability to tune material 
properties through detailed electroplating processes bridges 
the long-standing gap and fills in gaps in the materials selection in mechanical design space between polymer and metal 
AM parts. This novel research represents a shift in AM by 
transforming what was once considered a limitation of SLS 
printing—thin-wall anisotropy—into an opportunity for 
creating customized material properties through strategic 
metal deposition, but also opens up new design spaces where 
minimum weight and minimum volume design trajectories 
are needed. The results of this study can be applied to many different 
industries to improve, and tune material properties of printed 
parts to fit a specific application. One of those applications 
is structurally scaled ship models and two papers by Ibrahim 
et al. investigated applying the discussed techniques to create structurally scaled ship models for hydro-elastic model 
test experiments [33, 34]. This type of experiment is geared 
toward measuring global design loads on ships and their 
structural response [35, 36]. To achieve the desired scaled 
structural stiffness, the models must have relatively large 
overall dimensions with very thin thickness (0.8 mm) for the 
structural members (Fig. 1). Electroplating the model using 
the methods discussed in this paper results in increasing the 
model structural stiffness while maintaining the very thin 
thickness of structural members. Furthermore, electroplating the model creates a watertight layer to eliminate moisture absorption during testing in a towing tank. This paper 
includes calculations to predict performance of such models 
enabling both the geometry and the stiffness to be appropriately scaled.

section: 2.1 Design of experiments A design of experiments (DOE) was developed to analyze
text_for_embedding:
[s40964-025-01386-w | Additive Manufacturing / Materials | 2.1 Design of experiments A design of experiments (DOE) was developed to analyze | p.4]
2.1 Design of experiments
A design of experiments (DOE) was developed to analyze 
electroplating effects on the tensile properties of PA12 parts 
manufactured using SLS. The DOE focused on establishing 
methods to compare the isotropy of plated (electroplated) 
and unplated SLS parts. Tensile characterization from a previous study by Slager et al. was leveraged to set the baseline 
for unplated tensile data [10]. To achieve a direct comparison 
Fig. 1 Hydro-elastic ship model 
fabricated using SLS with 
0.8 mm PA12 wall thickness 
and coated with a three-part 
electroplating process

892
 

to the unplated study, tensile specimens printed during the 
initial study were plated and analyzed. The printed batch 
included 144 ASTM-D638 tensile specimens [37] with 24 
specimens in each orthotropic orientation (Fig. 2a). Each 
orientation included 12 standard specimens (3.2 mm thickness) and 12 thin specimens (0.8 mm thickness). The standard and thin samples were of the same dimensions with the 
exception of specimen thickness. To further isolate changes 
in material properties to orientation, thickness, and plating, 
all specimens were printed in the inner 60% of the build 
chamber and a constant x direction hatch pattern without 
perimeters was used (Fig. 2b). A naming convention was 
adopted to distinguish between print orientation, thickness, 
and plating. A two-letter identifier described the orientation, where the first letter identified the axial (pull direction) 
and the second letter identified the transverse direction of 
the tensile specimen. The specimens were further classified 
as 'standard' or 'thin' to denote thickness, and 'unplated' or 
'plated' to indicate electroplating status.

2.2 Additive manufacturing
All specimens were printed in a single build using a Fuse 1 
SLS printer manufactured by Formlabs (Formlabs, Somerville, MA). The Fuse 1 utilizes a 10W fiber laser with a 200 
microns spot size and an ambient air build chamber with 
temperatures up to 200° C. Specimens were orientated and 
arranged within the build area using Autodesk (Autodesk, 
San Francisco, CA) Netfabb AM software (version 2024). 
The build file was sliced using Formlabs PreForm slicing 
software (version 3.29). Laser power and hatch pattern can 
affect the mechanical properties of SLS parts [38]. PreForm 
minimizes mechanical property changes by adjusting laser 
speed based on cross-section through a patent-pending “Surface Armor” technology. Print settings matched a previous 
study by Slager et al. [10] to achieve a direct comparison 
to uncoated material properties. A layer height of 0.11 mm 
and a constant x-direction hatch pattern without perimeter 
matched the study done by Slager et al. (Fig. 2b). Laser 
power, recoater direction, and temperature profile were also 
held constant for all samples to further isolate the effects of 
print orientation and match the previous uncoated study by 
Slager et al. (Fig. 2) [10].

2.4.2 Electroplating materials
Electroplating materials selected for coating the sintered 
PA12 tensile specimens were sequentially layered equal 
parts of structural copper [Cu(s)], a ductile nickel bath 
(Traditional Nickle Sulfamate [TNS]), and hard nickel bath 
(Nickle deposit with a platinum anode [NDPA]). Nominal 
plating thickness was 0.0045” (114 microns) based on total 
current (amp-hours/foot2) and time in each bath. A separate 
bath was used for each material. Copper was deposited first 
as electroplating tests on SLS parts demonstrated its superior tolerance to the relatively rough powder surface. The 
thickness of each material layer was measured using two 
methods. First, by measuring the cross-section of the gauge 
section before and after electroplating. Second, by weighing each specimen before and after plating and calculating 
the plated material volume using the known density of each 
material and assuming uniform coating thickness. The thickness of each material was calculated by dividing total plate 
thickness by number of material baths (assumed equal thickness of each material).

2.5 Mechanical testing of plating material
Material properties of these coatings were experimentally 
determined using microtensile specimens. Traditional samples for characterizing materials are insufficient for determining the mechanical response of electrodeposits, since 
film properties are coupled to thickness and evolution of 
microstructure. If the standard ASTM D1708-02A sample, 
which is 38 mm x 15 mm with a gage section of 5 mm by 
3 mm, was used, property evolution due to the manufacturing process would be lost, because the thickness of the sample is beyond the evolution of the grain texture [56]. Zupan 
et al. developed a novel microsample that enables investigation on a much smaller length scale [57, 58]. This study used 
a similar testing geometry with an overall sample dimension 
of 3 × 1 mm and a gage section of 250 x 250 µm [59–61]. 
Characterization of the evolution of the coating is possible, 
because this sample allows independent measurements of 
the properties in both the growth direction and the transverse 
direction. Figure 3 shows the micro-material testing system 
(µ-MTS) (Fig. 3a) and a micro-tension sample (Fig. 3b). A 
non-contact laser-based interferometric strain/displacement 
gage (ISDG) was used. Strain rates of 1 × ­10–4 per second 
were used for all samples.

2.5.1 Microsample extraction/ fabrication
Microsamples were extracted from nickel and copper electrodeposited films approximately 4 mm thick (Fig. 4). The 
samples were cut using plunge electron discharge machining (EDM). This process has been shown to yield samples 
with a repeatable accurate cross-sectional tolerance to within 
0.1 µm. The samples were extracted in two specific orientations: the transverse direction (TD) and the growth direction (GD). This allows characterization of how the material 
properties change with respect to orientation.

2.6 Mechanical testing under tensile loading
Tensile testing was conducted using ASTM D638-22 TypeV [37] uniaxial tensile test standards for all samples with 
a crosshead rate of 1 mm/min. Prior to testing, all samples 
were maintained in a 73.4 ± 3.6°F; 50 ± 10% relative humidity laboratory environment for at least 40 h. The samples 
were then measured at three distinct cross-sectional planes 
for width and thickness before testing in accordance with 
ASTM-D618 [62].
The tensile testing was performed using an Instron 
(Instron, Norwood, MA) Model 4466 screw driven test 
frame with a Model 2518–806 load cell (verified tensile 
range of 1.00–200lbf) to apply and resolve force. Specimen 
grips were reinforced with a single layer of 120-grit Norton 
Metalite (Saint-Gobain Industries, Staverton, Gloucestershire) abrasive paper. Due to the use of digital image correlation for longitudinal deformation measurements, the 
specimen gauge section was painted. Following specimen 
preparation, the specimens were mounted in the Instron by 
centering and restraining each specimen within serrated parallel face grips with sufficient applied pressure to preclude 
slippage during force application. A non-contacting digital 
imaging correlation system was used to obtain longitudinal deformation measurements. The system consisted of 
an Imetrum (Imetrum Limited, Bristol, UK) Model SC-2 
processor and an Allied Vision (Allied Vision, Thuringia, 
Germany) Mako Model G-192B PoE camera with Imetrum 
Video Gauge Version 5.4.8 (Build 6128) software.

results
The grain structure for the TNS deposited nickel was determined to be 786 nm, while the NDPA nickel has a grain size 
of 74 nm. This grain reduction is consistent with strengthening due to a Hall–Petch type mechanism in which the 
strength scales proportional to the inverse square root of the 
grain size [3, 31]. Strength is increased, because the path of 
motion of the dislocations is reduced, such that once they 
glide across the smaller grain center, they are impeded or 
pinned by the grain boundaries.
Figure 6 shows the inverse pole figures and grain size 
distributions for the NDPA nickel starting from the substrate 
through 1.5 mm of growth. A series of 3 scans were taken 
to characterize the NDPA nickel at various lengths from the 
substrate. The first scan was taken in the first 5–15 µm of 
the sample, the second scan was taken at 1 mm, and the 
third scan was taken at 1.5 mm above the substrate. Each 
scan was enhanced using CI standardization followed by one 
iteration of grain dilation. The grain size and morphology 
of the NDPA nickel material evolves in size as you traverse 
the growth direction. In the first 5–15 µm, the grain size is 
measured as small as 20 nm for the average grain size in 
the scan. The grain morphology evolved from equiaxed to 
slightly elongated grains, with the major axis aligned with 
the growth direction. This increase in grain size along the

897
 
growth direction correlates with decreased strength in the 
metallic coating as thickness increases. The elongated grain 
structure introduces material anisotropy. The grain elongation direction oscillates between 10 and 15 degrees relative 
to the growth direction. This alternating grain orientation 
promotes grain rotation as a primary deformation mechanism, resulting in reduced strain-to-failure as energy is dissipated through rotation rather than grain boundary sliding. 
The inverse pole figures also give light into the directionality of the electrodeposits. The growth direction for NDPA 
nickel trends toward < 201 > texture directions. The texture 
relaxes slightly toward the < 100 > direction as the coating 
grows. This texture inside of the material can change the 
plastic response and result in a higher yield point for the 
growth direction.
Texture was also analyzed for the TNS to see if the trends 
followed for both electrodeposited materials. Figure 7 shows 
the texture for both NDPA nickel and TNS nickel. In this 
figure, the same scale is used for both samples and the scale 
was switched to linear to make direct comparisons of the 
Fig. 5 Representative curve for

two materials. The TNS sample appears to have minimal to 
no texture preference.

3.3 Coated sintered PA12 tensile test results
The mechanical testing performed on the 18 coated standard 
samples and 18 coated thin samples followed the same procedures previously done by Slager et al. on uncoated samples [10] to allow a direct comparison between the coated 
and uncoated samples. Uncoated data, that were previously 
published by Slager et al. [10], are incorporated in the tables 
(Tables 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7) and figures (Figures 9, 10, 11, 12) 
of these coated results to facilitate a direct comparison and 
discussion on the advantages and disadvantages of electroplating SLS parts. ­EA, σy, UTS, and ϵf were determined and 
individually analyzed below. Stress–strain curves were generated for a selection of the fractured samples to provide representative graphs that allowed a comparison of the impacts 
of thickness and print orientation on stress and strain. A 
consolidated stress–strain graph showing coated samples 
of both standard and thin thickness is provided in Fig. 8. Follow-on graphs and tables are presented that compare the 
effects of sample thickness and print orientation on ­EA, σy, 
UTS, and ϵf. 3.3.1 Axial elastic modulus ­(EA)
A graphical representation of the effects of thickness, 
print orientation, and electroplate coating on ­EA is provided in Fig. 9 and Table 3 numerically presents the same 
results. The uncoated data were part of a prior study [10], 
while the coated data represent the electroplated samples. This graph shows that the coated samples all had a significantly higher stiffness than their uncoated counterparts. In 
general, the coated standard samples for the XY, XZ, YX, 
and YZ print orientations had a slightly higher stiffness 
than the ZX and ZY print orientations. For the coated thin 
samples, the XY and YX samples had the highest stiffness. Overall, the average ­EA for the coated thin samples 
was 41,859 MPa which was 94% higher than the average 
­EA of 21,611 MPa for the coated standard samples. Of the 
coated samples, the thin YZ orientation had the highest 
­EA (46,884 MPa) and the standard ZY orientation had the 
lowest ­EA (19,443 MPa). When comparing the coated and 
uncoated samples, the coated thin sample average ­EA value 
(41,859 Mpa) is over 30 times higher than the uncoated 
thin sample average ­EA value (1258 MPa) and the coated 
standard sample average ­EA value (21,611 MPa) is over 13 
times higher than the standard sample uncoated average 
­EA value (1578 MPa). It should be noted that for coated 
samples, the thin samples had the highest ­EA across all print 
orientations and for the uncoated samples, the opposite was 
true as the standard samples had the highest ­EA across all 
print orientations. To support a clearer comparison between 
coated and uncoated sample specimen variability, the relative standard deviation was determined with the relative 
standard deviation being less than 10% for all thicknesses 
and all print orientations. ANOVA analysis indicated that 
there was a statistically significant difference of ­EA based on 
orientation for all samples except the thin coated samples. Based on t tests statistical analysis, the standard coated samples were slightly less dependent on orientation with 7 pairs 
(XY–XZ, XY–YX, XY–YZ, XZ–YX, XZ–YZ, YX–YZ, 
and ZX–ZY) being statistically the same as opposed to the 
uncoated standard samples which had 5 pairs being statistically the same (XY–XZ XY–YX, XY–YZ, XZ–YX, 
and YZ–ZX).

3.3.3 Ultimate tensile strength (UTS)
A graphical representation of the effects of thickness, 
print orientation, and electroplate coating on UTS is provided in Fig. 11 and Table 5 numerically presents the same 
results. This graph shows that the coated samples all had a 
significantly higher UTS than their uncoated counterparts. For both the standard and coated thin samples, the XY, XZ, 
YX, and YZ print orientations all had a higher UTS than 
the ZX and ZY print orientations. Overall, the average UTS 
for the coated thin samples was 239.7 MPa which was 99% 
higher than the average UTS of 120.2 MPa for the coated 
standard samples. For the coated samples, the thin XY orientation had the highest UTS (251.9 MPa) with the all of the X 
and Y print orientations having similar UTS values and the 
standard ZY orientation had the lowest UTS (102.3 MPa). When comparing the coated and uncoated samples, the 
coated thin sample average UTS value (239.7 MPa) was 
over eight times higher than the uncoated thin sample average UTS value (28.7 MPa) and the coated standard sample 
average UTS value (120.2 MPa) was a little over three times 
the uncoated standard sample average UTS (39.5 MPa). In 
alignment with the results for ­EA and σy, the coated thin 
samples had the highest UTS across all print orientations 
and for the uncoated samples. Conversely, uncoated standard 
thickness samples exhibited higher UTS values across all 
print orientations compared to uncoated thin samples. To 
quantify specimen variability between coated and uncoated 
samples, the relative standard deviation was calculated and 
found to be less than 8% across all thicknesses and print 
orientations. ANOVA analysis again indicated that there was 
a statistically significant difference of UTS based on orientation for all samples except the thin coated samples. Based 
on t tests statistical analysis, the standard samples were less 
dependent on orientation with 5 pairs for both uncoated 
(XY–XZ, XY–YX, XZ–YX, YX–YZ, and ZX–ZY) and 
coated (XY–XZ, XY–YZ, XY–ZX, XZ–YZ, XZ–ZX) having no statistical difference as opposed to the uncoated thin 
samples which only had 3 pairs with no statistical difference (XY–YX, XZ–YZ, and ZX–ZY). Similar to ­EA and 
σy results, when comparing print orientation and sample 
thickness it was clear that sample thickness and coating had 
a larger impact on UTS than print orientation. 3.3.4 Strain at failure (ϵf)
A graphical representation of the effects of thickness, 
print orientation, and electroplate coating on ϵf is provided 
in Fig. 12 and Table 6 numerically presents the same results. This graph shows that the coated samples all had a significantly lower ϵf than their uncoated counterparts. In general, 
ϵf is not significantly different for the various print orientations of the coated samples. Overall, the average ϵf for the 
coated thin samples was 1.57%, which was only slightly less 
than the average ϵf of 1.70% for the coated standard samples. When comparing the coated and uncoated samples, 
the coated thin sample average ϵf value (1.57%) was over 
three times lower than the uncoated thin sample average ϵf 
value (5.40%) and the coated standard sample average ϵf 
value (1.70%) was over four times lower than the uncoated 
standard sample average ϵf (7.62%).

3.5 Coated sintered PA12 material ROM property 
prediction results
ROM (Eqs. 1, 2) was used to calculated predicted values 
of ­EA, σy, and UTS and compared to the tested values 
discussed in Section 3.2. Measuring the gauge cross-section before and after plating resulted in a 17.3 and 35.7% 
coated material for the standard and thin specimens, 
respectively. For all coatings used, the metallic coating 
was vastly stiffer and stronger than the PA12, and so, the 
ROM results were largely driven by the coating properties. 
The predicted values (calculated using the ROM equation), 
with a comparison to the experimental values, are listed 
in Table 8. ­EA predictions match much better than σy and 
UTS. The ­EA prediction was within 10% for orientations 
on the build plate and went up to 23% for the thin ZY orientation. However, overall ­EA prediction average was well 
under 10% for both the standard and thin specimens. Thin 
specimens predicted material values matched the experimental values closer than the thick specimens. σy and UTS 
predictions were much less accurate than ­EA predictions 
with an average deviation of 36–54%. UTS predictions 
were slightly better than σy and thin specimen predictions 
were slightly better than standard specimen predictions. 
­EA data (property well within the elastic regime) indicate 
the feasibility of using ROM to predict material properties. 
However, σy and UTS data do not correlate well enough 
with ROM calculations to effectively predict these properties using ROM.

3.6 Coated sintered PA12 cross‑sectioned 
microscopy results
Specimens were sectioned to compare pre-fracture cross-section (Fig. 13) and fractured cross-section (Figs. 14 and 15). 
The process of sectioning tended to damage the cross-section 
and influence the results, so multiple methods were used to 
support characterization. Using a slow speed circular diamond 
blade at room temperature (Fig. 13a) and a razor blade pushed 
through the section as a wedge after soaking the sample in 
liquid nitrogen (Fig. 13b-c) resulted in the least amount of 
cross-section and material interface damage during sectioning. The sectioning done at room temperature did not indicate 
any separation at the PA12/coating interface; however, plastic deformation (“smearing”) of the PA12 made it difficult to 
identify the interface. Sectioning at cryogenic temperatures 
(Fig. 13b-c) mitigated most of the plastic deformation during sectioning but did appear to cause some damage that may 
have pulled the PA12 away from the coating. Figure 13c also 
appears to show three distinct layers (electroplating materials) 
in the coating. In all cases, it does appear the coating filled 
in most of the rough particulate SLS surface and bonded to 
the PA12 core. Though voids and under-sintered particles are 
evident in both of the cryogenic sections (Fig. 13b-c), these 
print defects are much more pronounced in the thin section 
(Fig. 13b). Globular hemisphere-like growth on the surface of 
the coating can be seen on all sections. The size of the globular shapes is much larger than the PA12 particle size and is 
consistent with other work describing these globular features 
during electroplating [17]. In both images, the coating appears 
to fill in the particulate surface of the printed part as well as 
fill in any edge defects.

3.7 Coated sintered PA12 specimen fractography 
results
The tensile specimen fracture surfaces were analyzed using 
SEM to identify and evaluate factors that may have contributed to the evaluated material properties and anisotropy. The 
internal sintered PA12 specimens were imaged to qualitatively identify voids, porosity, and particle adhesion/sintering. The uniformity, adhesion, and geometry of the coating 
were also analyzed to investigate the interaction between the 
sintered PA12 and electroplated metal coating during tensile 
loading. Figure 14 is a fracture image at 100x magnification 
of the coated standard samples at each different print orientation and Fig. 15 is a fracture image at 100x magnification 
of the coated thin samples at each different print orientation.
All fracture surfaces were relatively flat and appear to 
have little plastic deformation at the fracture surface. Standard samples orientation ZX and XZ (Fig. 14) have some 
areas of what appears to be ductile cup and cone fracture, 
but still with very little overall plastic deformation. Thin 
samples indicate similar areas that are most pronounced in 
YX, ZX, and YZ (Fig. 15), but the formations appear to be 
more stretched fibrils than cup and cone. Though the overall fracture mode appears to be relatively brittle for both 
the sintered PA12 and the metal coating, when compared to 
the sectioned samples (Fig. 13), it does appear the sintered 
PA12 core elastically deformed more than the metal coating 
which caused debonding at the PA12/metal interface. The 
Fig. 13 SEM 100 × and 200 × of sectioned coated samples using a slow speed diamond blade saw at room temperature and b-c razor blade 
wedge after soaking specimen in liquid nitrogen

907
 
debonding and pulling away of the PA12 from the metal 
coating was less pronounced in the Z orientation (ZX and 
ZY) for both standard and thin samples. In general, the overall interface debonding also appeared to be less pronounced 
in the thin samples than the standard samples. Some of 
the thick samples (XY and ZX) also appear to have some 
debonding within the metal coating.
Consistent with the sectioned images (Fig. 13), the standard samples (Fig. 14) appear to have more uniform sintering 
with no noticeable unsintered particles. The thin samples 
(Fig. 15) in comparison tend to have more sintering defects 
(noticeably porosity and under-sintered particles). Globular 
formations on the surface of the coatings are also present 
(similar to the sectioned specimens).

4 Discussion and future direction
This research demonstrates a novel hybrid materials 
approach combining SLS with strategic electroplating to 
dramatically enhance part performance while mitigating 
traditional SLS limitations. Through a novel electroplating 
process using copper and two distinct nickel depositions, 
this work accomplished improvements in mechanical properties—including elastic modulus and yield strength, while 
reducing print orientation anisotropy.
Mechanical characterization of electroplating microsamples with a footprint of 3 mm x 1 mm and a gauge section 
of 250 µm x 250 µm allow investigation into the properties 
in the growth direction as well as the transverse direction. 
It was found that the copper deposited FCC material had no 
directional dependence and behaved very isotropically, while 
the nickel deposited materials had variations in the two 
directions tested. In addition, both materials showed significant strengthening when compared to other manufacturing 
Fig. 14 SEM 100 × magnification of coated standard samples

908

processes, such as casting or extrusion of the base metals. 
This was linked to grain refinement down to sub-100 nm for 
the deposition process. Nickel materials that were deposited 
with supplemental platinum anodes have strength exceeding 
two times that of traditionally electrodeposited nickel. A significant number of grains in the NDPA nickel measure below 
50 nm with the possibility to reduce size further through 
precise control of the supplemental anodes. The justification 
for the strengthening was related back to the grain structure 
of the materials with anisotropy being related to the texture of the deposits. The reason for the varying properties 
of the coatings for the nickel materials was related back to 
slight residual compressive stress in the nickel deposits as 
well as grain texture and evolution. The grains grow larger 
in diameter as they increase in distance from the substrate. 
This results in a higher propensity for larger weaker grains 
as material deposits become thicker. Grain texture in the 
growth direction heavily favors the < 201 > directions, 
which also explains the change in properties of the growth 
direction as only 2 of the 12 FCC slips systems are active for 
the NDPA nickel. The properties measured are very useful 
for functionalization of electrodeposited structures formed 
from 3D-printing, as the base substrate can be designed to 
take advantage of the unique texturing that occurs within 
the material. While ROM can serve to guide the structural 
enhancement of coated polymers, finite-element optimizations can be varied for directional properties as well as 
thickness-dependent properties. It is hypothesized that 
diminishing returns will occur for electrodeposited materials, since the grain size is linked to the thickness of the 
coating. Iterative processes will most likely be required to 
optimize mechanical structures using electrodeposition as 
the primary strengthening phase.
Reductions in strength for the growth direction NDPA 
nickel can be attributed to grain evolution. Grains approximately 250 µm from the substrate have an average size of 
74 nm, while grains 1.5 mm from the substrate are 120 nm 
in diameter. The samples extracted from this portion fail in 
Fig. 15 SEM 100 × magnification of coated thin samples

[s40964-025-01386-w | Additive Manufacturing / Materials | 4 Discussion and future direction (Part 2/4) | pp.20–22]
the gage section; however, they fail near the thicker section 
of the deposit. This is due to larger gains present in this area. The resultant strength of the material is much lower at the 
larger grain size. The cause of the increase in grain size is 
attributed to columnar grains forming within the deposit. These grains tend to grow in diameter as they progress. The 
columnar grains do not span the full length of the deposit 
but grow in a columnar fashion for a brief period. The phenomenon regulating this is not yet well understood but is 
postulated to be related to the grain surface energy of noncolumnar grains. Increasing both tensile properties and isotropy hinged on 
achieving uniform and strong adhesion between the nonmetallic printed material and the metallic coating. The high 
throw acid copper bath appeared to place relatively complex 
geometries (Fig. 1) while filling the voids of the SLS powder 
surface (Fig. 13). The initial acid copper bath formulations 
used aided in coating corners and slots and provided good 
metal filling into the relatively rough SLS surfaces. This 
was additionally improved by the slow plating rates used 
which appears to also aid in bridging copper across fine 
gaps. These findings show promise of adding electroplating 
to SLS design for AM without incorporating expensive and 
extensive post-processing such as vapor smoothing. Further investigation is still warranted to find techniques that 
increase coating uniformity and adhesion while decreasing 
globular formations on exterior surfaces. Tensile results of the coated sintered PA12 specimens 
showed a significant increase in tensile properties from 
uncoated to coated as well as a decrease in anisotropy. Similar to previous research done by Slager et al. [10], inconsistencies in sintering are more pronounced in the thin samples; 
however, electroplating filled in the edge defects and reduced 
the ­DoA due to print orientation. Sample thickness and coating had a larger impact than print orientation and average 
DoA was reduced for all tensile properties when the specimen was coated. ­EA for standard specimens experienced the 
smallest increase in isotropy with coating. However, coating significantly decreased DoA due to orientation for all 
other specimens and material properties. Most properties 
benefited from at least a 50% decrease in DoA and strain at 
failure saw the largest decrease in DoA going from approximately 50% uncoated to around 10% coated (Table 7). While 
the ANOVA and t test analysis did not definitively identify 
the impact of orientation of print orientation on coated samples with the samples used, the incorporation of ­DOA analysis more clearly highlighted these impacts. Future research 
with an increased sample size (larger than the three used for 
this study) could provide further insight into whether a difference more definitely exists. Overall, fractography and sectioning indicated the separation between the PA12 and metal coating occurred during 
plastic deformation. Z orientations tend to be more brittle 
[10] resulting in less debonding during fracture. This orientation also experienced some of the greatest benefit in 
strength and mitigated some of the disadvantage of stressing 
a part in the build direction. Still, the results do indicate that 
the difference in stiffness between the metal and the PA12 
will likely cause debonding if the sample is deformed well 
into the plastic regime (σy and UTS, respectively).

however, electroplating filled in the edge defects and reduced 
the ­DoA due to print orientation. Sample thickness and coating had a larger impact than print orientation and average 
DoA was reduced for all tensile properties when the specimen was coated. ­EA for standard specimens experienced the 
smallest increase in isotropy with coating. However, coating significantly decreased DoA due to orientation for all 
other specimens and material properties. Most properties 
benefited from at least a 50% decrease in DoA and strain at 
failure saw the largest decrease in DoA going from approximately 50% uncoated to around 10% coated (Table 7). While 
the ANOVA and t test analysis did not definitively identify 
the impact of orientation of print orientation on coated samples with the samples used, the incorporation of ­DOA analysis more clearly highlighted these impacts. Future research 
with an increased sample size (larger than the three used for 
this study) could provide further insight into whether a difference more definitely exists. Overall, fractography and sectioning indicated the separation between the PA12 and metal coating occurred during 
plastic deformation. Z orientations tend to be more brittle 
[10] resulting in less debonding during fracture. This orientation also experienced some of the greatest benefit in 
strength and mitigated some of the disadvantage of stressing 
a part in the build direction. Still, the results do indicate that 
the difference in stiffness between the metal and the PA12 
will likely cause debonding if the sample is deformed well 
into the plastic regime (σy and UTS, respectively).

coat the low-density area and possibly offer some smoothing 
before the nickel builds a good reinforcing layer. A second 
complication between the core PA12 material and the metal 
coating is the difference in stiffness. The metal coating is 
often > 70 times stiffer than the plastic core. The difference 
in strength and stiffness is one of the primary advantages of 
coating SLS parts, but the present electroplating research 
has found that thin electroplated layers on soft substrates 
do not reinforce as well as thin electroplated layers on more 
rigid materials. The difference in stiffness and strength may 
cause some delamination at higher strains, but the mismatch 
in stiffness also often plastically loads the metal coating 
before the polymer core. Typically, at < 2% strain, the metal 
is fully loaded and the polymer core is only at ~ 20% of the 
load-carrying capacity. This can lead to the internal polymer elastically elongating and taking a small fraction of 
the load until the metal fractures, at which point the load 
is instantaneously transferred to the polymer resulting in 
immediate failure of the total structure. This phenomenon 
essentially results in sequential plastic regime loading of 
first the metal coating and then the polymer core. However, 
this research shows that this phenomenon may actually be 
swapped for some SLS build orientations resulting in the 
core PA12 failing before the metal coating. This highlights 
the importance of additional research when coating SLS 
parts because of the print orientation dependent material 
properties. Further investigation is needed to understand 
and optimize the difference between mechanical testing 
determined and predicted values for σy (41–48%) and UTS 
(33–42%), potentially through improved surface preparation, 
interface analysis, and techniques to improve and control 
metal–polymer bonding. Developing electroplating methods 
to ensure thickness uniformity around different part features 
especially between thin features (such as the gauge section 
in the Type-V tensile specimen) and thicker features (such 
as the grip section in the tensile specimen) may increase the 
predictability of total parts.

section: 5 Conclusion This research establishes a novel approach to addressing (Part 1/2)

[s40964-025-01386-w | Additive Manufacturing / Materials | 5 Conclusion This research establishes a novel approach to addressing (Part 1/2) | p.23]
5 Conclusion
This research establishes a novel approach to addressing 
fundamental limitations in polymer additive manufacturing through strategic electroplating. By developing a novel 
three-layer metallic coating process, we have not only 
achieved unparalleled increases in mechanical properties 
but also effectively mitigated the long-standing challenge of 
print orientation anisotropy for thin samples (0.8 mm) across 
all tested material properties and orientations indicated by a 
low ­DOA (3.5–12.0%) and ANOVA analysis showing no statistical difference in material properties based on orientation. Standard samples also showed a noticeable decrease in anisotropy for plastic deformation properties as indicated with 
average ­DOA decrease from 21.1% to 10.2% for UTS and 
55.0% to 10.8% for ϵf. This also highlights the importance of 
incorporating ­DOA analysis and not simply using more classical methods such as ANOVA and t tests as the decrease in 
anisotropy was not immediately apparent when using these 
methods. Overall, though both AM and electroplating are 
inherently anisotropic, if employed together correctly, they 
can decrease the anisotropy of the final multi-material part. The collected data also demonstrate the significance 
of electroplating thin and thick PA12 SLS specimens to 
improve tensile properties. Electroplated samples’ tensile 
properties ­(EA, σy, UTS) were all significantly higher than 
uncoated samples with the properties of the coating driving 
overall performance ­(EA increased 1270% for standard and 
3230% for thin samples, σy increased 220% for standard and 
750% for thin samples, and UTS increased 200% for standard and 740% for thin samples). The increase in ­EA, σy, and 
UTS did come at the cost of decreased εf which is attributed 
to the stiffer nature of the coating as compared to the base 
material (εf decreased 350% for standard and 250% for thin 
samples). When comparing print orientation and sample 
thickness, it is clear that sample thickness and coating had 
a larger impact on ­EA, σy, and UTS than print orientation. Strain at failure had the opposite effect, but results varied 
less based on orientation when compared to uncoated samples. The success of this approach, particularly with thinwalled structures, demonstrates that the inherent trade-off 
between lightweight design and mechanical performance in 
polymer AM can be overcome through controlled metallization, while maintaining the cost and weight advantages that 
makes polymer AM attractive. The implications of this work extend beyond the immediate mechanical property improvements measured and 
reported. Electroplating also opens the door to customizing 
part properties by calculating required coating thickness 
using ROM, which was demonstrated for ­EA with an average 
deviation from ROM predicted values to measured values 
of 5.2% for standard samples and 7.5% for thin samples. ROM was not as accurate of a material property prediction 
tool for properties further in the plastic region, such as σy, 
UTS, and εf. suggesting that further research is prudent to 
expand this predictive capability beyond ­EA. Overall, the 
study demonstrated that it is possible to create hybrid disparate phase polymer–metal components with predictable and 
tunable properties through control of electroplating parameters and grain structure refinement.

paper_title: Analysis of the thermal design of a COTS-based modular battery system for satellites by thermal vacuum testing
text_for_embedding:
[s12567-023-00526-8 | Spacecraft / Battery Thermal Management | Abstract | N/A]
Abstract
The qualification of components for satellite applications is a costly process due to the extreme conditions that must be 
endured in space. Therefore, space market access of battery technology innovations is often inhibited. However, modern 
battery technologies offer great advantages for satellite applications. In this work, a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) based 
and modular lithium-ion battery system for satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) is presented. A comparative analysis to 
evaluate system parameters and functionality of the proposed battery system and literature data is performed. A thermal 
vacuum test campaign is carried out to investigate the behaviour under LEO relevant conditions and to achieve qualification 
of the system performance according to the ECSS (European Cooperation for Space Standardization) standard. The tested 
system consists of two modules with 28 V nominal voltage and eight battery cells each. Experiments were conducted inside 
a vacuum chamber. The battery system was charged and discharged in temperatures from 0 °C to 45 °C in a high-vacuum for 
three weeks. The influence of the battery management electronics, the behaviour of the cells and the heating were analyzed. 
The cell temperatures stayed in the operating limit during 3.5 A and 10 A cycling. The battery system, however, exceeded the 
cell’s upper operating limit with a 40 °C baseplate and 3.5 A charging. Despite the dense system architecture with electronics 
between the cells the battery system can safely deliver power in a broad temperature range. Further investigations regarding 
safety and failure modes are necessary, along with advancements on software and state estimation algorithms.
Keywords Battery management system · Thermal vacuum · Thermal qualification · Satellite power

1 3
without sunlight during the orbit around Earth. Furthermore, a satellite’s battery is used in the Launch and Early 
Operations (LEOP) phase and as a buffer for high-power 
consumers. Nowadays, lithium-ion (Li-ion) battery cells are 
typically applied due to their high volumetric and gravimetric energy density (of up to 250 Wh/kg) compared to other 
battery chemistries [1, 2]. The Li-ion cell, however, has disadvantages. The materials are rare, difficult to mine and toxic [3, 4]. Their minimum 
voltage (2.5 V) and maximum voltage (4.2 V) must not be 
exceeded to guarantee safe operation. In addition, the cell 
shall be stored between – 20 °C and 60 °C and operated 
between 0 °C and 40 °C for most variants. Violating these 
limits can lead to reduced lifetime, outgassing or even fire 
[5]. Lastly, the lifetime or cycle stability of a Li-ion cell 
depends on the operation. A satellite in Low Earth Orbit 
(LEO) will experience around 6000 charge–discharge cycles 
just in a year [6]. Generally, the Li-ion satellite batteries 
of the past decade have worked successfully in-orbit for 
multiple years. They do so by reducing depth-of-discharge 
(DOD), EoCV (End of Charge Voltage), state of charge 
(SOC), current and avoiding temperature extremes [7]. The Li-ion battery for spacecraft was initially demonstrated in the Proba-1 mission [8]. The satellite, that originally was designed for one year, has now operated successfully for over 20 years with a battery system not exhibiting 
any battery monitoring or management. In ref. [8] the performance of the Li-ion battery systems of the Proba-1 and 
Mars Express missions is analyzed with ABSL in-house 
performance prediction tools. In general, the authors point 
out that the understanding of the changing behavior of the 
battery system over varied missions is crucial for an optimal battery sizing and with that a maximization of weight 
savings. Since the flight on Proba-1 the Li-ion battery cell was 
validated as power storage for spacecraft and improved in

exceeded to guarantee safe operation. In addition, the cell

depends on the operation. A satellite in Low Earth Orbit 
(LEO) will experience around 6000 charge–discharge cycles 
just in a year [6]. Generally, the Li-ion satellite batteries 
of the past decade have worked successfully in-orbit for 
multiple years. They do so by reducing depth-of-discharge 
(DOD), EoCV (End of Charge Voltage), state of charge 
(SOC), current and avoiding temperature extremes [7]. The Li-ion battery for spacecraft was initially demonstrated in the Proba-1 mission [8]. The satellite, that originally was designed for one year, has now operated successfully for over 20 years with a battery system not exhibiting

With the application 
of a battery management system (BMS) in such systems 
mitigation of space debris can be achieved by following 
the standards for satellite applications [14]. A disbalance 
of the battery cells can lead to failure or worse [5]. Lastly, 
the knowledge on the SOC and state of health (SOH) of 
the battery cells gives the satellite operator more insight for 
problem solving or operations planning [15]. Especially for 
satellites, which cannot receive maintenance, an additional 
improvement and knowledge of the remaining battery lifetime is beneficial [16]. An overview of available literature data of Li-ion-based 
battery systems for satellites is shown in Table 1. The data 
are taken from refs [17–20]. Among the 22 named battery systems there are small ones 
that are focused on the CubeSat market and larger ones that 
are used in small and medium satellites. The smaller systems 
generally follow the COTS approach whereas the medium 
and large systems follow a more robust and conservative 
selection of components. A simple balancing approach is implemented in 8 of the 
cited battery systems, which are both small and large systems. In those systems the cells are balanced over a shunt 
resistor at one prefixed voltage. Adaptive EoCV is offered 
by two systems. Four battery systems offer SOC calculation via coulomb 
counting. One offer SOH monitoring. Most systems do not state a radiation tolerance level. For 
five of the systems the TID value is between 20 and 30 krad, 
which allows 5-year LEO missions. An outlier is a battery 
system that offers radiation tolerance of up to 3000 krad. The approach of using non-space qualified COTS electronic components and battery cells leads to higher efforts 
for qualification and testing under relevant conditions. In 
contrast, high energy densities (> 120 Wh/kg at battery 
system level), more functionality and lower prices can be 
achieved. There are also battery systems successfully flying 
in satellites that do not use battery management and balancing. The drawback is that these systems need more focus 
on battery cell selection and battery cell testing. The cells 
must to have the same interior resistances or a behaviour that 
keeps them balanced. The early Li-ion powered satellites 
relied on a specific mechanism of decreasing self-discharge 
with increasing SOC in their selected cell [21]. In this work, a modular COTS-based battery system is 
presented to achieve a first proof-of-concept. Its behaviour under thermal loads and vacuum relevant conditions

battery cells and structure. An autonomous BMS is applied.

printed circuit board (PCB) that is in contact with the battery 
cells and also serves the structural integrity of the system. A 
market study supports the systems beneficial energy density 
and functionality considerations [22]. Thermal vacuum tests 
are conducted to investigate the system’s behaviour under 
space-relevant conditions and to validate the conceptual 
approach.

2.1 Space environment
The environmental conditions and requirements to the battery system are a result of the mission and orbit of the satellite. The focus of this paper is on the vacuum condition and 
the temperatures that a battery system experiences in LEO.
The temperature of a spacecraft is influenced by four 
sources of energy [23]. The different radiation sources are 
visualized in Fig. 1. These are the Sun, Earth’s albedo, 
Earth’s infrared radiation and the internal electronic 
hardware. The Sun’s solar flux goes directly to the hull 
of the satellite. The albedo is a fraction of solar energy 
which is reflected by Earth. Furthermore, Earth’s surface 
absorbs radiation from the Sun. It then reemits a part of 
the energy as infrared. Lastly, the hardware onboard the 
satellite produces waste heat. The incoming energy then 
exchanges in form of heat between the satellite’s shell and 
interior hardware like a battery system.

text_for_embedding:
[s12567-023-00526-8 | Spacecraft / Battery Thermal Management | 2.2 Modular smart battery system (MSBS) (Part 1/3) | pp.5–6]
2.2 Modular smart battery system (MSBS)
To achieve a modular and scalable architecture, the MSBS, 
proposed in this work, consists of separated battery modules connected in parallel by the surrounding structure. Each 
module contains battery cells, electronics and structural elements. The aspect of modularity is described in detail in a 
previous work [22]. In Fig. 2 the first prototype consisting of 
two parallel modules is shown. The PCBs with electronics 
are directly connected with the battery cells and include all 
necessary components to manage the cells. The aluminium 
thermal elements and structure elements are also visible. The PCBs also act as structural components and give stability to the system. The system delivers a nominal voltage of 28.8 V (with 
maximum of 33.6 V and minimum of 20 V), a maximum 
current of 10 A short term (< 1 min) and a continuous current of up to 3.4 A. In Fig. 3 the volumetric and gravimetric energy densities 
of systems from literature are compared to the presented 
single module and the systems with structure and two or four 
modules. The MSBS with added battery management and 
compact structural elements exhibit high system energy. The 
battery modules use commercial components that are available in high quality at an affordable price (most components 
are below 10 €). The battery cells used are standard cells in 
the 18,650 size. The battery system contains a BMS that balances the serially connected cells, monitors the charging and discharging currents and analyses the operating status of the cells. The values and status messages can be communicated via 
Controller Area Network (CAN) or Universal Asynchronous Receiver–Transmitter (UART) to the onboard computer (OBC), power control and distribution unit (PCDU) or 
even shared between the modules. Additionally, a command 
can be sent to the modules to change operation of balancer, 
heater or state machine. The centrepiece of the BMS is a microcontroller that is 
programmed with the software and commands the other 
electronic components like temperature sensors, current 
sensor and heaters. A balancing unit individually measures 
and balances each cell voltage at any value. Moreover, there 
are components for communication via CAN, temperature 
measuring, current measuring, latch-up protection, voltage 
regulation, heating and a back-up balancer. These components have either been previously tested for radiation or have 
a rad-hardened counterpart. The software of the system, 
which runs the battery management, checks the sensors and 
runs a state machine. With this state machine the temperature, current and voltages of the battery cells are monitored, 
analyzed and managed. In case of an error or emergency 
possible actions are heating, balancing, reset of the system 
or ignoring a faulty sensor. The battery system contains one temperature sensor on 
each battery cell. The temperature sensors are communicating with the microcontroller on a one-wire bus. The onboard 
software communicates the monitored temperature at a resolution of 1 °C. A higher resolution for the temperatures of 
up to 0.0625 K can be requested via CAN. The structure components inside the battery modules are 
part of the thermal system (Fig. 2). There are cell holders 
that physically connect the battery cells with the PCBs and 
hold everything in place. The cell holders are 3D-printed 
with polyether ether ketone (PEEK).

[s12567-023-00526-8 | Spacecraft / Battery Thermal Management | 2.2 Modular smart battery system (MSBS) (Part 2/3) | pp.5–6]
This material was 
selected for its low weight and good electrical isolation 
properties. The thermal surface between the battery cells 
and the outside structure is improved by the integration of 
Fig. 2 Battery system with two battery modules and surrounding 
structure. Battery cells (pink), PCBs (green), thermal elements blue, 
structure elements (grey

515
Analysis of the thermal design of a COTS‑based modular battery system for satellites by thermal…
1 3
thermal wedges, which are placed between the battery cells 
and are in direct contact with them and the structure. The 
thermal wedges are milled from aluminium, which is used 
for its good thermal conductivity. The aluminium wedges 
are not in contact with any of the battery cell’s poles. A 
thermal paste is used to reduce the contact resistance of the 
connection between thermal wedges, battery cells and PCBs.
The cell holders, thermal wedges, and included heater 
elements can be seen next to the battery cells and PCBs in 
Fig. 4. The system is thermally and structurally connected 
to the satellite via the aluminium boards at each end of the 
system. They can also be seen in Fig. 4.
To prevent the module of too cold temperatures four 
heaters are implemented into the thermal structures on each 
module. The aim of this thermal design is to ensure that the 
battery cells can be operated in an acceptable temperature 
window in a satellite environment.
The functionality and modern components used in the 
system must not add fatal errors. The system was, therefore, designed redundant. A simple FMEA with failures of 
the most important components of the BMS is presented in 
Table 2. Generally, the battery cells can always be charged 
and discharged, even if the BMS is not powered or failed. 
In case of an onboard electronics failure the cells are still 
operable. A backup balancing based on analog shunts will 
work without the BMS. Two additional temperature sensors 
on each module can be read out by an external system like 
the Onboard Computer (OBC) or PCDU. Failure of a module can be compensated by additional modules and failure 
of a sensor can be compensated by the other sensors. As the 
battery system is powered externally and not by itself there 
is also an additional layer of safety. In case of malfunction 
the BMS can simply be deactivated.

the Onboard Computer (OBC) or PCDU. Failure of a module can be compensated by additional modules and failure 
of a sensor can be compensated by the other sensors. As the 
battery system is powered externally and not by itself there

The battery system was placed in the vacuum chamber and 
held constantly under vacuum for three weeks. The vacuum 
chamber is equipped with a vacuum pump and has a thermostat attached to it. The additional equipment consists of 
a remotely accessible laptop with LabVIEW as control and 
automation platform, an electrical source–sink combination 
(EA PSB 9080–120 with 0–120 V and 0.1% precision), a 
CAN dongle (PCAN-USB IPEH-002021 with 250 kbits/sec) 
and a battery tester (Basytec Cell Test System). With the laptop every test device of the setup can be controlled and the 
communication with the two battery modules in the vacuum 
chamber is routed to the laptop via CAN. The source–sink is 
used to charge and discharge the battery system. The 28 V 
supply simulates the power supply of the battery management’s electronics. This enables an external reset of the BMS 
electronics. The battery cells are not connected to this and 
can still be charged or discharged if the voltage supply is 
turned off. Lastly, the battery tester was used to read out 
additional external temperature sensors. Eight external temperature sensors were placed on the battery system. Figure 6 
shows their positions. Two of them are placed on the legs 
of the structure close to the baseplate (1,2). Two sensors 
are placed inside the thermal elements (3,4). Two additional 
external sensors are placed next to on-board sensors (5,6,7) 
to validate the temperature measurement on the battery cells. 
The last external sensor is placed inside the top module at 
the pole of a cell (8).
The collected data via CAN bus include current, voltages and temperatures of the system. Additionally, status messages that describe the system state (charging, 
discharging, idle, balancing and emergency) and the 
status of the balancer and heater are logged. Every five 
seconds a dataset is collected via CAN bus and stored on 
the laptop. In addition, voltage and current of the source 
and sink were measured. Therefore, each measured value 
of the onboard sensors can be compared to the external 
measurements. With this setup the temperatures and currents could be changed remotely and the system can be 
monitored at any time.

The temperature of the thermal baseplate can be controlled with a heat transfer fluid. This fluid is regulated from 
the outside by a thermostat. Before insertion into the vacuum 
chamber the setup was additionally surrounded by a thermal 
shroud. The thermal shroud reflects thermal radiation back 
to the battery system. The baseplate simulates the mechanical interface and thermal conduction with the satellite. The 
shroud simulates the thermal radiation inside of the satellite. 
The satellite interfaces and in-orbit temperatures could deviate from the test setup. However, the connection and thermal 
management of the satellite are usually designed to benefit 
the most sensitive components.
The temperatures of the baseplate were changed during 
the test according to the test plan. The temperature of the 
shroud was also monitored and was within 4 K of the baseplate after the dwelling and during the tests.
The goals for the thermal-vacuum test campaign are as 
follows:
• Prove operation of battery cells in thermal-vacuum.
• Prove functionality of electronics in thermal-vacuum.
• Test battery system under different static temperatures 
during charging and discharging.
• Understand thermal behaviour and heat distribution of 
the battery system during operation.

section: 3.2 Testing process The thermal-vacuum campaign was based on to the ECSS
text_for_embedding:
[s12567-023-00526-8 | Spacecraft / Battery Thermal Management | 3.2 Testing process The thermal-vacuum campaign was based on to the ECSS | p.9]
3.2 Testing process
The thermal-vacuum campaign was based on to the ECSS 
standard [26, 27]. At first a non-operational cycle was conducted. In this the baseplate and system were tempered to 
the non-operational limits ( – 20 °C and 60 °C). Then the 
temperatures were held (dwelling). In the non-operational 
cycle the battery cells were not charged or discharged, but 
the monitoring and BMS was turned on.
Thereafter seven operational cycles were conducted. 
For each of the seven operational cycles (thermal cycles) 
the operational maximum (40 °C) and the operational 
minimum (0 °C) were approached and held. After each 
temperature change, once the temperature had settled, 
charging and discharging of the battery system was conducted (electrical cycles). During the whole campaign a 
two-hour dwelling was conducted after each temperature 
change. The dwelling was only started if all temperatures 
were measured within 1 K or beyond the goal temperature. 
For the operational maximum 40 °C instead of 45 °C was 
chosen due to the heating from the cells during the electrical cycling.
Charging and discharging was conducted with the two 
battery modules connected in parallel. The system’s battery cells were charged and discharged at a baseplate fixed 
temperature after the dwelling was completed. Two different 
currents were applied during the tests. One cycle consisted 
of discharging and charging of the battery system. The battery cells were charged to 32.8 V, which is the product of 
eight serial battery cells at 4.1 V (approx. 90% SOC). The 
charging process consisted of a constant current (CC) phase 
and a constant voltage (CV) phase until a charging current 
of 300 mA was undershot.
At least four cycles for each temperature–current combination were carried out to give the system time to approach 
a thermal equilibrium.
The temperature ranges for the battery system are limited 
by the temperature limits of the battery cells themselves. 
Li-ion cells generally have two temperature ranges. The nonoperational temperature range for storing the cells, usually 
ranges from – 20 °C to 60 °C [28]. The operational range is 
between 0 °C and 45 °C for charging and broader for discharging ( – 20 °C to 60 °C). The operational range is smaller 
because the cells are additionally stressed internally. These 
temperature limits must not be exceeded during the test or 
the operation due to safety reasons. There is an optimal 
range for operating between 10 °C and 35 °C. Anything that 
goes far from this causes an accelerated aging of the cells 
[29]. The eight thermal cycles including the temperature 
changes and dwell times took about ten days of continuous 
monitoring and testing. Additional tests included discharging at – 20 °C and 55 °C and tests for the heating and balancing. The aspired pressure inside the vacuum chamber is at 
­10–6 mbar or lower.
The stability of the microcontroller and electronics were 
also tested and evaluated during the thermal vacuum test 
campaign. The on-board data logging, processing and communication and the functions of the electronics like heating and balancing were tested. The system temperatures are 
monitored (Table 3).

[s12567-023-00526-8 | Spacecraft / Battery Thermal Management | 4.1 Influence of current on temperature (Part 1/2) | p.10]
4.1 Influence of current on temperature
Figure 8 shows the results of the electrical cycling during 
the 40 °C operational test of a thermal cycle. The measurements of current and temperatures of the external sensors 
in relation to the testing time are visible. The test started 
at 40 °C baseplate temperature (therefore simulating a 
40 °C connection interface to the satellite). The temperature control for the extreme temperatures is hard to achieve 
with losses between thermostat and baseplate. Therefore, 
a more extreme temperature was also accepted to start the 
dwelling or cycling. The measured current is the module current which flows through each cell. In the graph 
five cycles are depicted. One cycle consists of charging 
and discharging. The discharging leads to a temperature 
increase.
The temperatures also increase during CC phase. 
During the CV phase the temperatures decrease. The 
pronounced temperature increase during discharge and CC 
phase is the consequence of the heat dissipation that stems 
from the current flowing through the cells and their interior resistances. The temperatures decrease slightly during 
the CV phase as the current through the battery cells and 
therefore the heat dissipation is rapidly decreasing. During 
that phase the thermal conduction away from the battery 
cells is greater than the thermal heat dissipation generated 
inside of the battery cells due to the internal resistance.
The baseplate and, therefore, the emulated satellite are 
heated to 40 °C. This can be seen in the baseplate connection sensors, which stays between 41–42 °C for the whole 
test as it is very close to the baseplate. It also has to be 
noted that there are temperature differences between certain 
parts of the battery system. Firstly, a temperature difference 
of around 1 K can be seen between baseplate and the battery system’s structure. Further, a temperature difference of 
around 1.5 K can be observed between the structure and the 
thermal elements. Finally, a gap in temperature of below 1 K 
between the thermal elements and the battery cells is visible.
Altogether, the temperature increases during the first 
two cycles. At the beginning of the experiment the overall 
temperature increase is pronounced. After cycle three, an 
equilibrium seems to be reached. This means that a thermal 
balance between inflowing energy in the form of dissipated 
heat from cells and electronic is almost equal to the outflowing energy via thermal conduction and thermal radiation. 
Conduction and radiation of heat to the outside increase with 
rising temperature. It is assumed that both processes contribute to the equilibration.
The maximum temperature difference between baseplate 
and battery cells amounted to 4.5 K in this particular test.

cells is greater than the thermal heat dissipation generated 
inside of the battery cells due to the internal resistance.
The baseplate and, therefore, the emulated satellite are 
heated to 40 °C. This can be seen in the baseplate connection sensors, which stays between 41–42 °C for the whole 
test as it is very close to the baseplate. It also has to be 
noted that there are temperature differences between certain 
parts of the battery system. Firstly, a temperature difference 
of around 1 K can be seen between baseplate and the battery system’s structure. Further, a temperature difference of 
around 1.5 K can be observed between the structure and the 
thermal elements. Finally, a gap in temperature of below 1 K 
between the thermal elements and the battery cells is visible.
Altogether, the temperature increases during the first 
two cycles. At the beginning of the experiment the overall 
temperature increase is pronounced. After cycle three, an 
equilibrium seems to be reached. This means that a thermal 
balance between inflowing energy in the form of dissipated 
heat from cells and electronic is almost equal to the outflowing energy via thermal conduction and thermal radiation. 
Conduction and radiation of heat to the outside increase with 
rising temperature. It is assumed that both processes contribute to the equilibration.
The maximum temperature difference between baseplate 
and battery cells amounted to 4.5 K in this particular test.

During the test campaign the heaters were tested with 
a CAN command from outside and the operation of the 
system was monitored. The resulting temperature profile 
of the battery cells and the activity of the heater over time 
are shown in Fig. 11. The consumption of the heaters is at 
0,7 W per module. The four heaters were able to increase 
the temperature of the system by around 0.75 K in 10 min. 
The temperature sensor recognizes the heater-on after one 
minute due to the distance between them. The heaters are 
working against the active cooling of the baseplate that is 
kept at 0 °C by a thermostat. If a cold start of the system 
below 0 °C occurs (during LEOP or emergency) discharging 
the system is fine as the operational limits are broader for 
discharging. After discharging the cells can only be charged 
if the operation was able to increase the cell temperature 
above 0 °C. Alternatively, the heater is able to lift up the 
initial cell temperature. During operation it can be assumed 
that the heating is able to keep cell temperatures above 0 °C 
if they start to drop below.
Cell balancing was also tested. The balancing of eight 
cells induces around 7 W of waste heat into the system. The 
balancing is generally only conducted at the end of a charge 
cycle on a few cells for several seconds. In this test the worst 
case was simulated and the balancing was continuously run 
for 30 min on all eight cells to see the heat development in 
case of a failure. The temperatures of the cells rise by around 
12 °C to 15 °C in that timeframe.

5 Conclusions
A thermal vacuum test campaign was conducted on a COTSbased modular Li-ion battery system. The thermal behaviour of two battery modules with 28 V nominal voltage and 
eight battery cells each was investigated inside a vacuum 
chamber. The battery system was operated in temperatures 
from – 20 °C to 55 °C in a high-vacuum for three weeks.
The thermal-vacuum (TVAC) test campaign proves the 
functionality of the battery system under LEO-relevant conditions. All cells worked properly during the tests. The dense 
system architecture with electronics between the cells the 
battery system was able to safely deliver power in a broad 
temperature range.
To verify the electronic functionality and working, external sensors were mounted to measure voltage, current and 
temperature values, the values from external sensors coincided with the values from sensor onboard. The software 
Fig. 10 External temperature sensor vs Onboard temperature sensor
Fig. 11 Operation of heater and 
influence on the battery cells

522
 

1 3
also worked properly and constantly delivered data and 
telemetry. It also processed external inputs. Throughout the 
test, the temperature of the battery cells was monitored.
The thermal management worked effectively and kept the 
battery cells in their temperature range. A temperature difference of around 5 K between the baseplate and the battery 
cells was observed during operation with 3.5 A. For higher 
currents the cell temperature increase is more pronounced 
resulting in a higher temperature difference between cell and 
base plate. The cell temperatures fell below the operating 
limits below 0 °C. Heating was tested for those temperatures. 
However, heating takes a long time to bring the cell temperatures up. Additionally, the heating tests were not sufficient to 
verify at which temperatures and for how long they would 
be able to raise the temperatures of the system.
For the tests with 3.5 A the limits were overshot at 40 °C 
baseplate temperature. The higher-power cycling with 10 
A was only possible at 0 °C and 20 °C. The temperature 
behaviour seems to be in line with reports of other authors 
[30, 31].
Further investigation and research are essential to address 
safety and failure modes in the proposed battery system. Due 
to the inclusion of electronics and software it is crucial to 
ensure the system does not endanger the satellite’s mission. 
Additionally, advancements on software and state estimation 
algorithms of the system need to be made. This will contribute to enhancing the overall performance and reliability of 
the battery system for satellite applications.
Moving forward, there are several aspects for future publications. The radiation test campaigns conducted on the 
electronic components of the system will be analyzed and 
published. Additionally, upcoming projects on low temperature missions and the integration of post-lithium battery cells 
(for specific applications) will leverage the scientific value 
of the presented modular battery system.

Bremen for providing insight with a thermal analysis and thanks to 
Thilo Glaser from DLR-SY in Braunschweig for the support with the 
battery system’s structure.

available from the corresponding author, Marius Eilenberger, upon 
reasonable request.
